opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's going to change quite a lot, and quite quickly. We're already seeing these coding assistants become genuinely useful. They're not just autocompleting a line here or there; they can write whole functions and, increasingly, whole modules. So the value of the kind of programming that is mostly translating a well-specified idea into syntax is going to go down. That's just going to get automated, in the same way that very few people write assembly anymore.

But I don't think that means programming skill becomes worthless. Quite the opposite in some ways. What becomes more valuable is the higher-level stuff: knowing what to build, how to architect a system, how to decompose a problem, how to judge whether what the AI has produced is actually correct and elegant, or just superficially plausible. You still need deep understanding to supervise these systems well. If anything, the people who really understand the fundamentals, computer science, algorithms, the maths underneath, will be supercharged, because they'll be able to direct ten or a hundred times more output than before.

I also think it opens programming up to a lot more people. Natural language is becoming a kind of programming interface. Designers, scientists, artists, people who have great ideas but never had the time to learn all the arcane details of a particular language, will be able to build things. That's very exciting to me. When I was young, making games, a huge amount of the effort was just wrestling with the machine. If you can remove that friction, creativity and taste become the bottleneck, and that's a good place for the bottleneck to be.

So my advice to young people would still be: learn to code, learn it deeply, but also get really comfortable with these tools, because the combination of genuine understanding plus fluency with AI is going to be incredibly powerful. And develop your taste, your sense of what's an interesting problem worth solving. That part, I think, stays human for quite a while yet.

r001.rationale: The response says routine translation of well-specified ideas into syntax will lose value, while higher-level work such as architecture, problem decomposition, and deep technical understanding will become more valuable.

fable-5.1.text:
It's a question I think about a lot, partly because I came up through programming myself. I was writing games as a teenager, and the thing that got me into AI in the first place was writing code for Theme Park at Bullfrog and seeing how far a few clever rules could take you.

I'd separate programming into a few layers. There's the mechanical layer, which is translating a well-specified idea into working syntax. That's the part AI tools are already very good at, and it's going to keep getting better. Boilerplate, API glue, writing tests, porting between languages. I think the value of that kind of work as a standalone human skill is going to drop quite steeply, and honestly I don't think that's a tragedy. Most programmers never loved that part anyway.

Then there's the architectural layer. Deciding what the system should look like, how the pieces fit together, where the abstractions should go, what trade-offs you're willing to make. That's much harder for current systems, because it requires holding a lot of context in your head and understanding what the thing is actually for. I think that stays valuable for quite a while, but it changes character. You become more like a conductor than a performer. You're directing and reviewing and correcting rather than typing every note yourself.

And then there's a third layer that I think becomes more valuable, not less, which is really understanding the problem domain. If you're writing software for protein folding or for fusion plasma control or for a hospital scheduling system, the bottleneck increasingly isn't writing the code. It's knowing what the right question is, knowing what good looks like, and being able to tell when the output is subtly wrong. We saw this with AlphaFold. The deep learning expertise mattered enormously, but so did having people who really understood structural biology and could say, that structure looks plausible, that one doesn't.

So I'd say to a young person: learn to program, absolutely, because you need to understand the material you're shaping. But don't think of programming as the end product. Think of it as a way of thinking clearly about systems. The people who will do best are the ones who combine that computational mindset with real depth in something else, and who have the taste to judge whether what the machine produced is actually good.

The thing I'd caution against is the idea that it all just goes away. These tools make mistakes, they're confidently wrong, and verifying their output still requires somebody who could in principle have written it themselves. I think that remains true for a long time for anything that matters. But the kind of programming that's valuable is shifting from production towards judgment, and I think that's actually quite an exciting shift if you lean into it.

r001.rationale: The response says mechanical programming will lose value while the more difficult architectural work will remain valuable for quite a while, communicating that advanced programming may retain greater value than routine programming as AI improves.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish between writing code and engineering a system. A lot of the routine work—implementing a well-specified function, translating between languages, writing boilerplate—is going to become much easier with AI. That’s enormously valuable, because it allows more people to build things and lets experienced programmers explore ideas much faster.

But deciding what to build, choosing the right abstraction, understanding how the pieces fit together, and checking whether the system actually does what you intended—those remain difficult. Their relative value may actually increase as producing code becomes cheaper.

And then there’s programming as a way of thinking. I wouldn’t discourage someone from learning it. There’s something very powerful about learning to express an idea precisely enough that a machine can execute it. Even if you eventually delegate most of the implementation, that understanding helps you ask better questions and spot mistakes.

The really exciting possibility is that we spend less time wrestling with the mechanics and more time experimenting. You can have an idea and test it while it’s still fresh. But we need the tools to be reliable enough that the time saved writing code doesn’t simply become time spent finding subtle errors.

r001.rationale: The response says system design and judgment may gain value relative to routine code production, but it does not clearly identify cutting-edge programming as retaining greater value than other kinds of programming.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps to separate writing code from understanding what you want a system to do. AI tools will take on more of the routine implementation work, and that could make programming accessible to a much wider range of people. You can describe an idea, build a prototype, and explore it without first mastering every detail of a language.

But the difficult questions remain: What’s the right problem? What should the architecture be? How do you know the result is correct? Those require judgment and a deep understanding of the system. As generating code gets cheaper, those skills may become even more valuable.

And then there’s programming as a way of thinking. Learning to break a problem down, reason precisely, and test your assumptions is useful even if you’re no longer typing every line yourself. So I’d still encourage people to learn the fundamentals. The exciting possibility is that you spend less time on the mechanics and more time experimenting with ideas.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts routine implementation, which AI will increasingly handle, with difficult work such as choosing problems, designing architecture, and judging correctness, which it says may become more valuable as code generation gets cheaper.
